section.heading: 2.2. The Limit of a Function
section.paragraph: Having seen in the preceding section how limits arise when we want to find the tangent to a curve or the velocity of an object, we now turn our attention to limits in general and numerical and graphical methods for computing them.
section.heading: Finding Limits Numerically and Graphically
section.paragraph: Let’s investigate the behavior of the function $$f$$ defined by $$f(x) = (x - 1)/(x^{2} - 1)$$ for values of $$x$$ near $$1$$ . The following table gives values of $$f(x)$$ for values of $$x$$ close to $$1$$ but not equal to $$1$$ .

From the table and the graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 1 we see that the closer $$x$$ is to $$1$$ (on either side of $$1$$ ), the closer $$f(x)$$ is to $$0.5$$ . In fact, it appears that we can make the values of $$f(x)$$ as close as we like to $$0.5$$ by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to $$1$$ . We express this by saying “the limit of the function $$f(x) = (x - 1)/(x^{2} - 1)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$1$$ is equal to $$0.5$$ .” The notation for this is
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x - 1}{x^{2} - 1} = 0.5$$

note.title: Intuitive Definition of a Limit
note.heading: Intuitive Definition of a Limit
note.paragraph: Suppose $$f(x)$$ is defined when $$x$$ is near the number $$a$$ . (This means that $$f$$ is defined on some open interval that contains $$a$$ , except possibly at $$a$$ itself.) Then we write

if we can make the values of $$f(x)$$ arbitrarily close to $$L$$ (as close to $$L$$ as we like) by restricting $$x$$ to be sufficiently close to $$a$$ (on either side of $$a$$ ) but not equal to $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: Roughly speaking, this says that the values of $$f(x)$$ approach $$L$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ . In other words, the values of $$f(x)$$ tend to get closer and closer to the number $$L$$ as $$x$$ gets closer and closer to the number $$a$$ (from either side of $$a$$ ) but $$x \neq a$$ . (A more precise definition will be given in Section 2.4.)
An alternative notation for
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$
is
$$\left. f(x)\rightarrow L \right. {as} \left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$
which is usually read “ $$f(x)$$ approaches $$L$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ .”

Notice the phrase “but $$x$$ not equal to $$a$$ ” in the definition of limit. This means that in finding the limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ , we never consider $$x = a$$ . In fact, $$f(x)$$ need not even be defined when $$x = a$$ . The only thing that matters is how $$f$$ is defined near $$a$$ .

Figure 2 shows the graphs of three functions. Note that in part (b), $$f(a)$$ is not defined and in part (c), $$f(a) \neq L$$ . But in each case, regardless of what happens at $$a$$ , it is true that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Estimate the value of $$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}}$$ .
Solution The table lists values of the function for several values of $$t$$ near $$0$$ .
As $$t$$ approaches $$0$$ , the values of the function seem to approach $$0.1666666\ldots$$ and so we guess that
$$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9} - 3}{t^{2}} = \frac{1}{6}$$

section.paragraph: In Example 1 what would have happened if we had taken even smaller values of $$t$$ ? The table below shows the results from one calculator; you can see that something strange seems to be happening.

If you try these calculations on your own calculator you might get different values, but eventually you will get the value $$0$$ if you make $$t$$ sufficiently small. Does this mean that the answer is really $$0$$ instead of $$\frac{1}{6}$$ ? No, the value of the limit is $$\frac{1}{6}$$ , as we will show in the next section. The problem is that the calculator gave false values because $$\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}$$ is very close to $$3$$ when $$t$$ is small. (In fact, when $$t$$ is sufficiently small, a calculator’s value for $$\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}$$ is $$3.000\ldots$$ to as many digits as the calculator is capable of carrying.)
Something similar happens when we try to graph the function

of Example 1 on a graphing calculator or computer. Parts (a) and (b) of Figure 3 show quite accurate graphs of $$f$$ , and if we trace along the curve, we can estimate easily that the limit is about $$\frac{1}{6}$$ . But if we zoom in too much, as in parts (c) and (d), then we get inaccurate graphs, again due to rounding errors within the calculations.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Guess the value of $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}$$ .

Solution The function $$f(x) = \left( \sin x \right) \slash x$$ is not defined when $$x = 0$$ . Using a calculator (and remembering that, if $$x \in {\mathbb{R}}$$ , $$\sin x$$ means the sine of the angle whose radian measure is $$x$$ ), we construct a table of values correct to eight decimal places. From the table below and the graph in Figure 4 we guess that
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\left( {x^{3} + \frac{\cos 5x}{10,000}} \right)$$ .
Solution As before, we construct a table of values. From the first table below it appears that the limit might be zero.

But if we persevere with smaller values of $$x$$ , the second table suggests that the limit is more likely to be $$0.0001$$ . In Section 2.5 we will be able to show that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\cos 5x = 1$$ and that it follows that
$${\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\left( {x^{3} + \frac{\cos 5x}{10,000}} \right) = \frac{1}{10,000} =}0.0001$$

section.heading: One-Sided Limits
section.paragraph: The Heaviside function $$H$$ is defined by
$$H(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & {{if}t < 0} \\ 1 & {{if}t \geqslant 0} \end{cases}$$

(This function is named after the electrical engineer Oliver Heaviside [1850–1925] and can be used to describe an electric current that is switched on at time $$t = 0$$ .) Its graph is shown in Figure 5.

image.alt: Details A function with two parts is graphed on a coordinate plane. The first part of the function enters on the negative horizontal axis from the left, runs horizontally to the right, and ends at the origin with an open dot. The second part of the function begins at (0, 1) on the y axis with a solid dot and runs horizontally to the right in the first quadrant.

section.paragraph: There is no single number that $$H(t)$$ approaches as $$t$$ approaches $$0$$ . so $$\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}H(t)$$ does not exist. However, as as $$t$$ approaches $$0$$ from the left $$H(t)$$ approaches $$0$$ . As $$t$$ approaches $$0$$ from the right $$H(t)$$ approaches $$1$$ . We indicate this situation symbolically by writing
$$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{-}}H(t) = 0$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}H(t) = 1$$

and we call these one-sided limits. The notation $$\left. t\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ indicates that we consider only values of $$t$$ that are less than $$0$$ . Likewise, $$\left. t\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ indicates that we consider only values of $$t$$ that are greater than $$0$$ .

note.title: Intuitive Definition of One-Sided Limits
note.heading: Intuitive Definition of One-Sided Limits
note.paragraph: and say that the left-hand limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ [or the limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ from the left] is equal to $$L$$ if we can make the values of $$f(x)$$ arbitrarily close to $$L$$ by restricting $$x$$ to be sufficiently close to $$a$$ with $$x$$ less than $$a$$ .

and say that the right-hand limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ [or the limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ from the right] is equal to $$L$$ if we can make the values of $$f(x)$$ arbitrarily close to $$L$$ by restricting $$x$$ to be sufficiently close to $$a$$ with $$x$$ greater than $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: For instance, the notation $$\left. x\rightarrow 5^{-} \right.$$ means that we consider only $$x < 5$$ , and $$\left. x\rightarrow 5^{+} \right.$$ means that we consider only $$x > 5$$ . Definition 2 is illustrated in Figure 6.

section.paragraph: Notice that Definition 2 differs from Definition 1 only in that we require $$x$$ to be less than (or greater than) $$a$$ . By comparing these definitions, we see that the following is true.
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L {if and only if} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = L} {and} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = L}$$

section.heading: How Can a Limit Fail to Exist?
section.paragraph: We have seen that a limit fails to exist at a number $$a$$ if the left- and right-hand limits are not equal (as in Example 4). The next two examples illustrate additional ways that a limit can fail to exist.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Investigate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin\frac{\pi}{x}$$ .
Solution Notice that the function $$f(x) = \sin(\pi \slash x)$$ is undefined at $$0$$ . Evaluating the function for some small values of $$x$$ , we get

$$\begin{matrix} {f(1) = \sin\pi = 0} & {f\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = \sin 2\pi = 0} \\ {f\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = \sin 3\pi = 0} & {f\left( \frac{1}{4} \right) = \sin 4\pi = 0} \\ { f(0.1) = \sin 10\pi = 0} & {{f(0.01) = \sin 100\pi = 0}} \end{matrix}$$

Similarly, $$f(0.001) = f(0.0001) = 0$$ . On the basis of this information we might be tempted to guess that the limit is $$0$$ , but this time our guess is wrong. Note that although $$f(1 \slash n) = \sin n\pi = 0$$ for any integer $$n$$ , it is also true that $$f(x) = 1$$ for infinitely many values of $$x$$ (such as $$2 \slash 5$$ or $$2 \slash 101$$ ) that approach $$0$$ . You can see this from the graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 8.

image.alt: Details A sine function is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x and the y axes are displayed from negative 1 to 1 in increments of 1 unit. The curve labeled y = sin(pi/x), enters the third quadrant at approximately (negative 3, negative 0.7), goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches a low point in the third quadrant at approximately (negative 2, negative 1), then goes gradually up through the point (negative 1, 0), reaches its high point at approximately (negative 0.7, 1), and then falls to the approximate low point (negative 0.5, negative 1). It then oscillates multiple times between the y-values negative 1 and 1 until it reaches near the positive y axis. The graph then reflects its earlier path in the first quadrant by oscillating between the y-values negative 1 and 1, rising to a high point (0.5, 1), reaching its low point at (0.7, negative 1), then rising through the point (1, 0), concave down, and then goes down and to the right as it veers toward the x axis. The waves closer to the origin are closely spread and the waves away from the origin are widely spread.

example.paragraph: The dashed lines near the $$y$$ -axis indicate that the values of $$\sin(\pi \slash x)$$ oscillate between $$1$$ and $$- 1$$ infinitely often as $$x$$ approaches $$0$$ .
Since the values of $$f(x)$$ do not approach a fixed number as $$x$$ approaches $$0$$ ,
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\sin\frac{\pi}{x}{does not exist}$$

section.paragraph: Limits and Technology

Some software applications, including computer algebra systems (CAS), can compute limits. In order to avoid the types of pitfalls demonstrated in Examples 1, 3, and 5, such applications don’t find limits by numerical experimentation. Instead, they use more sophisticated techniques such as computing infinite series. You are encouraged to use one of these resources to compute the limits in the examples of this section and check your answers to the exercises in this chapter.

Examples 3 and 5 illustrate some of the pitfalls in guessing the value of a limit. It is easy to guess the wrong value if we use inappropriate values of $$x$$ , but it is difficult to know when to stop calculating values. And, as the discussion after Example 1 shows, sometimes calculators and computers give the wrong values. In the next section, however, we will develop foolproof methods for calculating limits.
Another way a limit at a number $$a$$ can fail to exist is when the function values grow arbitrarily large (in absolute value) as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ .

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}}$$ if it exists.

Solution As $$x$$ becomes close to $$0$$ , $$x^{2}$$ also becomes close to $$0$$ , and $$1 \slash x^{2}$$ becomes very large. (See the following table.) In fact, it appears from the graph of the function $$f(x) = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ shown in Figure 9 that the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made arbitrarily large by taking $$x$$ close enough to $$0$$ . Thus the values of $$f(x)$$ do not approach a number, so $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\left( {1 \slash x^{2}} \right)$$ does not exist.

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve y = 1/x^2 has two parts. The first part of the curve lies entirely in the second quadrant. It enters very close to the negative x axis from the left, goes up and to the right, veering away from the negative x axis, concave up, then continues to go upward to the right, and exits very close to the y axis at the top. The second part lies entirely in the first quadrant, mirroring the first part. It enters the first quadrant at the top near the positive y axis, goes down and to the right, concave up, then veers toward the positive x axis, and exits close to it.

section.heading: Infinite Limits; Vertical Asymptotes
section.paragraph: To indicate the kind of behavior exhibited in Example 6, we use the notation
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}} = \infty$$

This does not mean that we are regarding $$\infty$$ as a number. Nor does it mean that the limit exists. It simply expresses the particular way in which the limit does not exist: $$1 \slash x^{2}$$ can be made as large as we like by taking $$x$$ close enough to $$0$$ .
In general, we write symbolically
$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim}f(x) = \infty$$
to indicate that the values of $$f(x)$$ tend to become larger and larger (or “increase without bound”) as $$x$$ becomes closer and closer to $$a$$ .

$$\left. f(x)\rightarrow\infty \right. {as} \left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The vertical line $$x = a$$ is called a vertical asymptote of the curve $$y = f(x)$$ if at least one of the following statements is true:

$$\begin{array}{lll} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = \infty} & { {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = \infty}} & { {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = \infty}} \\ {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = - \infty} & { {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = - \infty}} & { {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = - \infty}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: For instance, the $$y$$ -axis is a vertical asymptote of the curve $$y = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ because $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}{({1 \slash x^{2}})} = \infty$$ . In Figure 12 the line $$x = a$$ is a vertical asymptote in each of the four cases shown. In general, knowledge of vertical asymptotes is very useful in sketching graphs.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Does the curve $$y = \frac{2x}{x - 3}$$ have a vertical asymptote?
Solution There is a potential vertical asymptote where the denominator is $$0$$ , that is, at $$x = 3$$ , so we investigate the one-sided limits there.

If $$x$$ is close to $$3$$ but larger than $$3$$ , then the denominator $$x - 3$$ is a small positive number and $$2x$$ is close to $$6$$ . So the quotient $$2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right)$$ is a large positive number. [For instance, if $$x = 3.01$$ then $$2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right) = 6.02 \slash 0.01 = 602$$ .] Thus, intuitively, we see that
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}\frac{2x}{x - 3} = \infty$$

Likewise, if $$x$$ is close to $$3$$ but smaller than $$3$$ , then $$x - 3$$ is a small negative number but $$2x$$ is still a positive number (close to $$6$$ ). So $$2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right)$$ is a numerically large negative number. Thus
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}\frac{2x}{x - 3} = - \infty$$
The graph of the curve $$y = 2x \slash \left( {x - 3} \right)$$ is given in Figure 13. According to Definition 6, the line $$x = 3$$ is a vertical asymptote.

image.alt: Details A vertical line and a curve are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The y axis is displayed from below 0 to beyond 5. The vertical line x = 3 is drawn from the first quadrant to the fourth quadrant, crossing the x axis at (3, 0). The curve y = 2 x/(x minus 3) has two parts. The first part enters the second quadrant near the x axis, goes down and to the right through the origin, concave down, enters into the fourth quadrant, approaches the vertical line x = 3, exiting the fourth quadrant at the bottom, very close to and to the left of x = 3. The second part lies entirely in the first quadrant to the right of x = 3. It enters the first quadrant at the top near the vertical line x = 3, goes down and to the right, concave up, veering toward the x axis, and exits near the right extreme of the x axis.

section.paragraph: NOTE Neither of the limits in Examples 6 and 7 exist, but in Example 6 we can write $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}{({1 \slash x^{2}})} = \infty$$ because $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$0$$ from either the left or the right. In Example 7, $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$3$$ from the right but $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$3$$ from the left, so we simply say that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 3}{f(x)}$$ does not exist.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Find the vertical asymptotes of $$f(x) = \tan x$$ .
Solution Because
$$\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$$

there are potential vertical asymptotes where $$\cos x = 0$$ . In fact, since $$\left. \cos x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\left( {\pi \slash 2} \right)^{-} \right.$$ and $$\left. \cos x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\left( {\pi \slash 2} \right)^{+} \right.$$ , whereas $$\sin x$$ is positive (near $$1$$ ) when $$x$$ is near $$\pi \slash 2$$ , we have
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow{(\pi \slash 2)}^{-}}\tan x = \infty$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow{(\pi \slash 2)}^{+}}\tan x = - \infty$$

This shows that the line $$x = \pi \slash 2$$ is a vertical asymptote. Similar reasoning shows that the lines $$x = \pi \slash 2 + n\pi$$ , where $$n$$ is an integer, are all vertical asymptotes of $$f(x) = \tan x$$ . The graph in Figure 14 confirms this.

image.alt: Details A tangent curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from negative 3 pi/2 to 3 pi/2 in increments of pi/2. The y axis is displayed from below 0 to beyond 1 in increments of 1 unit. Vertical lines parallel to the y axis are drawn at tick marks negative 3 pi/2, negative pi/2, pi/2, and 3 pi/2. The curve has multiple identical parts that are placed one after another, and each part lies between a pair of consecutive vertical lines. The first part of the curve enters from the bottom of the third quadrant, very near and to the right of the vertical line x = negative 3 pi/2, increasingly veering off it as the curve goes up and to the right, concave down, crosses the x axis at (negative pi, 0), continues rising upward to the right, now concave up, veering toward the dashed vertical line x = negative pi/2, and eventually exiting very near and to the left of it. The second part follows exactly the same movement, entering the third quadrant to the right and near the vertical line x = negative pi/2, passing through the origin, and exiting in the first quadrant to the left and near the dashed line x = pi/2. The third part lies between x = pi/2 and x = 3 pi/2, and crosses the x axis at (pi, 0).

section.paragraph: Another example of a function whose graph has a vertical asymptote is the natural logarithmic function $$y = \ln x$$ . From Figure 15 we see that
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\ln x = - \infty$$
and so the line $$x = 0$$ (the $$y$$ -axis) is a vertical asymptote. In fact, the same is true for $$y = \log_{b}x$$ provided that $$b > 1$$ . (See Figures 1.5.11 and 1.5.12.)

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve labeled y = ln(x) enters the bottom of the fourth quadrant near the y axis, goes up and to the right, concave down, crosses the positive x axis at (1, 0), and continues to go upward to the right in the first quadrant.

figure.caption: The $$y$$ -axis is a vertical asymptote of the natural logarithmic function.
